endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Require vendors to return or certifiably destroy all raw datasets, stop further training, and delete any models fine-tuned on your organizations data

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: ID.IM-P5: The purposes for the data actions are inventoried.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether a data acquisition register linked to an AI inventory reduces privacy, legal, or data quality problems, and no study documents how often untracked data flows occur. Support for the practice rests on two CHAI framework documents, so adoption is a governance judgment rather than an evidence-based finding.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies that test the practice and zero studies that document the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated when no comparative or observational data exist. The two endorsements are consensus statements from a single organization and do not substitute for measured outcomes.

Both endorsements come from CHAI frameworks. The Assurance Standards Guide asks that the purposes of data actions be inventoried, which is close to the register described here. The playbook's must-level item addresses vendor return or destruction of data. That duty may be easier to enforce when a register already records which datasets each vendor received.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares organizations with and without a data acquisition register on privacy incidents, audit findings, time to respond to data subject or regulator requests, or the completeness of vendor data return and deletion. No study measures the frequency or consequences of untracked data flows into clinical AI systems. Studies should also estimate the staff time needed to build and maintain a register at scale.
commentary.underserved_note: No test of the practice exists, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The supplied material cannot show whether a register would help health systems detect when these groups are missing from or underrepresented in training datasets.
